reviewer: Codex (AI-assisted focused assessment and distinct same-agent review)
scope: Review all 45 published countries for formal institutions being mistaken for effective democratic accountability. Ten focused corrections, not a new 240-answer independent research audit for each country.
measurementFinding: The unchanged bank awards democracy credit for rejecting expert, union or military appointment even in autocracies; suffrage and formal legislative constraints also receive independent credit. Consequently these percentages are quiz response balances, not a probability of democracy or a validated regime index. Corrected Iran remains 39.1% Democracy / 60.9% Autocracy; this review does not claim the underlying measurement distortion is fixed.
women: Coercive dress rules and repression concern Authority vs Liberty and the relevant social-policy questions. Exclusion from leadership, suppression of women’s political organisation and inability to challenge the governing establishment are relevant democracy evidence. No automatic cross-axis score transfer was applied.

changes.reason: Articles 59 and 110 make referendums dependent on parliamentary supermajority and leadership decree. This is not an implemented voter-controlled power to repeal a law; disagreement is qualified by the existence of binding institution-initiated referendums.

Article 110 places general policy and decisive appointments under supreme leadership. Subordinate executive and parliamentary work does not establish an independent veto over that paramount policy authority. The plural national leadership is assessed, without claiming the president alone decides everything.

Supreme authority is insulated from effective voter sanction; vetted representatives and the formal Experts removal provision do not establish independent accountability in practice. Internal clerical selection and removal are not equivalent to accountable popular representation.

Regular vetted presidential elections cannot renew or remove the supreme authority through genuinely competitive elections. Supreme leadership, not merely the subordinate presidency, is relevant to national leaders.

Article 76 parliamentary investigation does not give independent opposition access to the protected supreme-leader institutions and state-linked foundations. Exclusion of genuine opposition and immunity from scrutiny outweigh the formal investigative provision.

Constitutional review exists, but the supreme leader appoints the judicial head and controls Guardian Council selection. These dependent institutions do not supply the independent constitutional check required by the statement.

profiles.democracyEvidence: Vetted elections and an elected presidency coexist with supreme clerical authority and constrained opposition. Focused review prioritises implemented competitive renewal and effective oversight; formal powers in controlled institutions are not automatically democratic accountability.
profiles.counterEvidence: The March2026 succession used the Assembly of Experts; the president, supreme leader and armed forces have different constitutional powers, so restrictions are not assigned from a generic autocracy label. The bank also credits rejection of specific unelected alternatives (experts, unions, military) and narrower formal rights. These literal answers are retained where supported; the resulting percentage is not a probability or validated democracy index. Restrictions on women inform political participation where relevant, without automatically transferring Authority vs Liberty scores.

profiles.name: United States
profiles.period: Contemporary institutions and implemented policy; intended cut-off 2026-10-04
profiles.scope: 16 Democracy vs Autocracy questions reviewed; existing Authority vs Liberty and social-policy evidence checked for axis consistency. Other policy responses were not freshly independently researched.
profiles.outcome: Existing assessment retained after focused screening; not independently certified
profiles.democracyEvidence: The constitutional system selects national leadership through elections and divides legislative, executive and judicial authority. The 2026 election calendar, current party-qualification rules, September opposition spending inquiry, and February and June Supreme Court rulings provide dated implementation evidence. These support electoral and judicial constraints without assuming that formal checks always function effectively. State-level referendum and recall mechanisms are assessed separately from federal arrangements.
profiles.counterEvidence: Freedom House’s 2026 report covers 2025 and documents executive overreach, obstructed oversight and pressure on opponents; it is not treated as a report of events after its coverage period. FEC rules impose different ballot-support requirements on minor parties, so competition does not imply identical burdens. The September 2026 Democratic inquiry proves that opposition members can investigate and request information, not that their allegations are established or all requested records were provided. The June citizenship judgment supplies a constitutional judicial constraint; the February tariff judgment separately establishes limits on statutory delegation. Literacy and education tests are prohibited, but criminal-sentence and adjudicated-incapacity exclusions mean adult suffrage is not literally universal. Referendum and recall rights vary by jurisdiction.
